title: Penguins
text:
Data collected from: https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2026/2026-07-14
Original data from: https://opentraits.org/datasets/avonet.html


Code
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))


This dataset gives morphometric data for 18 species of penguins within 6 genera. In total, 93 penguins were surveyed.


Code
many_penguins <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-07-14/many_penguins.csv', show_col_types = FALSE)


ggplot(many_penguins, aes(x = beak.width, y = beak.length_culmen)) +
    geom_point() + 
    labs(
        x = "Beak width (mm)",
        y = "Culmen length (mm)",
        title = "Penguin beak width to culmen length relation"
    ) +
        facet_wrap(~species)









We can see that, for 6 of the species, there is little variation of culmen length and beak width. However, some species, such as eudyptes robustus. have quite a large variation in their culmen length and beak width. Overall, there is little relation between the two measurements.

This dataset shows dialogue from 3 of Shakespeare’s plays: Hamlet, Macbeth, and Romeo and Juliet. This project looks at how word usage differs between plays, which characters speak the most, and how frequently certain themes appear.
We want to answer the following questions:

title: Shakespeare Dialogue Analysis
text:
Loading data


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

hamlet <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/hamlet.csv")

macbeth <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/macbeth.csv")

romeo_juliet <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2024/2024-09-17/romeo_juliet.csv")

plays <- bind_rows(
  hamlet |> mutate(play = "Hamlet"),
  macbeth |> mutate(play = "Macbeth"),
  romeo_juliet |> mutate(play = "Romeo and Juliet")
)

plays <- plays |>
  filter(!is.na(dialogue), !is.na(character)) |>
  filter(!str_detect(character, regex("stage direction", ignore_case = TRUE))) |>
  mutate(
    dialogue = str_squish(dialogue),
    character = str_to_title(character),
    play = factor(play, levels = c("Hamlet", "Macbeth", "Romeo and Juliet")),
    word_count = str_count(dialogue, "\\b[A-Za-z]+\\b")
  )

title: Consecutive streaks
text:
Suppose you have a binary sequence: 00101101… that is \(n\) bits long (in other words, it contains \(n\) ‘digits’).
What is the possibility of observing a streak with at least \(k\) consecutive bits, given a total bit size of \(n\)? How does that value change with bias? That is, if probability of getting a 1 is no longer 0.5?
The applications of this simple question span can span from cryptography to gambling. For example, suppose you generate a cryptographyically secure pseudorandom number generator (CSPRNG), or a deterministic algorithm that generates random-looking numbers that are unpredictable enough for cryptographic use. If you weren’t sure if the generated number is biased, you could examine the frequency of certain streaks appearing in your generated value, and compare that to typical streaks of \(k\) bits in a simulation of the same size. You can also use the results to understand the probability of losing streaks in gambling. If there truly was a 25% chance to win at this game, is your losing streak of 10 expected, or are you extremely unlucky?
The answer to this question is surprisingly nontrivial to solve. Here, we try to answer this question by doing simulations.

Coin analysis
Suppose you have 2 coins, a fair coin, and a biased coin. The biased coin has a 60% chance to flip tails and a 40% chance to flip heads.
You want to find the probability of getting 20 consecutive heads when you flip a coin \(n\) times using both coins, and compare probability of the two. Is rolling it 10000 times using the fair coin likely going to give you 20 heads/tails in a row in any point in time? What about 15000 times? What if instead, we used the biased coin? At what number of rolls, do we have at least a 50% chance to get 20 heads/tails in a row using the fair coins?
Assume, for the sake of the simulation, that \(1\) represents heads, and \(0\) represents tails.
We start by defining a function simulate_streak(), which generates a random binary sequence of length \(n\). The function uses rle() to find the lengths of consecutive bits and checks whether any of those streaks are at least \(k\) bits long, and returns TRUE if such a streak exists and FALSE otherwise.
We then create a function estimate_prob() which uses map_lgl() to repeat the simulation num_trials amount of times. Since each simulation returns either TRUE or FALSE, we can take the mean of the results to estimate the probability of observing a streak of at least \(k\) bits. We use expand_grid() to create combinations of sequence lengths and probabilities of generating a 1, and map2_dbl() to run the simulations for each combination.


Code
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(47470)

sequence_lengths <- c(10000, 12000, 15000, 100000)
probabilities <- c(0.5, 0.4) 
k <- 20
num_trials = 10000

simulate_streak <- function(n, prob_one, k) {
  bits <- sample(
    c(0, 1),
    size = n,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = c(1 - prob_one, prob_one)
  )

  streaks <- rle(bits)$lengths

  any(streaks >= k)
}

estimate_prob <- function(n, prob_one, k, reps = num_trials) {
  results <- map_lgl(
    1:reps,
    \(x) simulate_streak(n, prob_one, k)
  )

  mean(results)
}

# runs simulations for each combination
results <- expand_grid(
  sequence_length = sequence_lengths,
  prob_one = probabilities
) |>
  mutate(
    streak_probability = map2_dbl(
      sequence_length,
      prob_one,
      \(n, p) estimate_prob(n, p, k)
    )
  )

results


# A tibble: 8 × 3
  sequence_length prob_one streak_probability
            <dbl>    <dbl>              <dbl>
1           10000      0.5             0.0086
2           10000      0.4             0.139 
3           12000      0.5             0.0102
4           12000      0.4             0.164 
5           15000      0.5             0.0159
6           15000      0.4             0.192 
7          100000      0.5             0.0888
8          100000      0.4             0.774 


Code
plot_results <- results |>
  filter(sequence_length != 100000)

ggplot(
  plot_results,
  aes(
    x = sequence_length,
    y = streak_probability,
    color = factor(prob_one),
    group = factor(prob_one)
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sequence_lengths) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of consecutive heads/tails",
    subtitle = paste0("Streak length of at least ", k, ", ran ", num_trials, " times"),
    x = "Number of flips",
    y = "Probability of a streak occuring",
    color = "Probability of heads"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()









(Note: length 100,000 is excluded from the plot)
From the plot, we see that, when the coin is fair, the probability of getting 20 heads/tails in a row is below 5% for all number of flips below 15,000. On the other hand, when the coin is biased, the probability of getting a 20 streak rises dramatically, hitting almost 20% for 15,000 rolls and 80% for 100,000 rolls.
An interesting result is how much a relatively small bias can affect the probability of observing long streaks. A slightly biased coin (60/40) was more likely to produce a 20 streak in 10,000 runs than a nonbiased coin in 10x the amount of runs. From a gambler’s perspective, if you are an insane losing streak, it’s much more likely that the game was rigged against you rather than the fact that you were simply just unlucky.

title: Birthday problem
text:
Birthday problem: In a room of n people, what is the probability that at least 2 people will share a birthday?
Although there are 365 days in a year, the unintuitive answer is that if there are just 23 people in the same room, there is over a 50% chance that two people share the same birthday. In this project, we will try to explain the unintuitive answer by running simulations that shows the probability that at least 2 people have the same birthday in a room of n people.
This simulation creates a function called simulate_birthday() that randomly assigns a birthday to each person in a room, assuming 365 equally likely birthdays. It then checks for matching birthdays using duplicated() and any(), returning TRUE if there is a match and FALSE otherwise. This process is repeated 5,000 times to estimate the probability of a shared birthday by calculating the proportion of successful matches. We then map this process using using map_dbl(), applying this process to room sizes ranging from 2 to 60 people, allowing us to see how the probability changes as the number of people increases.

title: Birthday problem
text:
Results


Code
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(4747)

num_of_people <- 2:60
num_of_runs <- 5000

simulate_birthday <- function(people) {
  birthdays <- sample.int(365, people, replace = TRUE)

  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

results <- tibble(
  people = num_of_people,
  probability = map_dbl(
    num_of_people,
    \(n) mean(replicate(
      num_of_runs,
      simulate_birthday(n)
    ))
  )
)

results |>
  filter(people %% 5 == 0)


# A tibble: 12 × 2
   people probability
    <int>       <dbl>
 1      5      0.0262
 2     10      0.109 
 3     15      0.264 
 4     20      0.413 
 5     25      0.571 
 6     30      0.696 
 7     35      0.814 
 8     40      0.891 
 9     45      0.939 
10     50      0.965 
11     55      0.984 
12     60      0.994 


Code
ggplot(results, aes(x = people, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "blue", size = 1) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Birthday problem",
    subtitle = "Simulated probability from 5,000 runs",
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Probability of at least 1 shared birthday"
  ) + theme_minimal()









The results show that the probability of a shared birthday increases rapidly as the number of people grows. At n=10 people, there is already a ~11.5% chance that 2 people share the same birthday, a very unintuitive number as there are 365 days in a year. At n=25 people, it’s a a ~56.6% chance that 2 people share the same birthday, and at n=50 people, it’s almost guaranteed that we have 2 people with the same birthday.
From the plot, we can see that the probability grows the most rapidly from 0 to around 35 people, then slows down as it approaches the asymptote of 100% probability. The unintuitive answer stems from the fact that we are not checking whether someone shares a birthday with one specific person, but whether any two people in the room share a birthday. As there are more and more people, the number of possible pairs increases rapidly, making a shared birthday much more likely than one might initially expect.
